etymology: From Greek plesion, “neighbour,” the parable our Lord spake to answer the lawyer’s question, Who is my neighbour?
biblical_def: A certain lawyer stood up and tempted Christ, saying, Master, what shall I do to inherit eternal life? (Luk 10:25); and being pointed to the law, he asked, willing to justify himself, Who is my neighbour? In answer the Lord told of a man who went down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and fell among thieves, which stripped him of his raiment, and wounded him, and departed, leaving him half dead (Luk 10:30). A priest and a Levite passed by on the other side; but a certain Samaritan, when he saw him, had compassion on him, bound up his wounds, set him on his own beast, and brought him to an inn, and took care of him (Luk 10:34). The dictionary marks this parable as our Lord’s exposition of the second great commandment, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself, which the lawyer would have narrowed to his own kind. Christ widens the neighbour to whomsoever I may help, and bids him, Go, and do thou likewise (Luk 10:37). Yet the parable was framed for a man seeking to be justified by doing; and the law’s full demand of a perfect, unceasing, self-spending love is a height no fallen man attains. So the Scripture teaches that the law, which saith, This do, and thou shalt live (Luk 10:28), drives the convicted sinner from his own works to the grace he cannot earn, and to Christ, the true Neighbour, who found us half dead and bound up our wounds.
webster_summary: The parable of the Samaritan who showed mercy to the wounded stranger, teaching the breadth of neighbour-love.
webster_full: THE GOOD SAMARITAN, the parable answering the lawyer’s question, Who is my neighbour?
A man going to Jericho fell among thieves and was left half dead.
A priest and a Levite passed by on the other side.
A Samaritan had compassion, bound his wounds, and cared for him.
Our Lord bids the hearer, Go, and do thou likewise.
scriptures: And he answering said, Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy strength, and with all thy mind; and thy neighbour as thyself.
And Jesus answering said, A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and fell among thieves, which stripped him of his raiment, and wounded him, and departed, leaving him half dead.
But a certain Samaritan, as he journeyed, came where he was: and when he saw him, he had compassion on him,
And he said, He that shewed mercy on him. Then said Jesus unto him, Go, and do thou likewise.
corruption_summary: The social-gospel reading detaches the parable from the lawyer’s question and the law’s demand, making it mere humanitarian works-righteousness.
corruption_paragraphs: This parable has suffered a real and widespread corruption in the progressive social gospel, which lifts it out of its frame and makes of it a bare lesson in humanitarian benevolence. The lawyer’s opening question, what shall I do to inherit eternal life, and our Lord’s closing word, this do, and thou shalt live, are quietly dropped; and the parable is preached as if good works of mercy were themselves the path to acceptance with God.

The dictionary names this for what it is: works-righteousness wearing the dress of compassion. Christ did not tell the parable to teach that men are saved by deeds of kindness, but to expose a self-justifying heart that would narrow the law’s demand to a manageable size. The law requires a love perfect, ceaseless, and whole, and by that standard the priest, the Levite, and the lawyer alike stand condemned, as do we. The full weight of this do, and thou shalt live is meant to break the sinner’s confidence in his own doing and drive him to the grace he cannot earn. So the parable is no charter for a social-gospel humanitarianism, but a tutor unto Christ, the true Neighbour, who had compassion on us when we lay half dead, and bound up our wounds at the cost of His own blood.
roots_summary: From the Greek for “neighbour,” the parable widens neighbour-love and drives the self-justifier to grace.
roots_lines: The Good Samaritan — from Greek plesion, “neighbour.”
It answers the lawyer’s question, Who is my neighbour?
A Samaritan shows mercy where priest and Levite passed by.
It expounds the second great commandment of neighbour-love.
Its law-demand drives the sinner to the grace he cannot earn.
usage: Like the Samaritan, the believer is bound to show mercy to whomsoever he may help.
He that shewed mercy on him. Go, and do thou likewise.
The law’s This do, and thou shalt live drives the sinner from his works to Christ.

etymology: From the Greek of Christ’s account in Luke, naming the beggar Lazarus (Hebrew Eleazar, “God hath helped”) over against the unnamed rich man.
biblical_def: Our Lord told of a certain rich man, which was clothed in purple and fine linen, and fared sumptuously every day; and a beggar named Lazarus, full of sores, laid at his gate (Luk 16:19; Luk 16:20). The beggar died, and was carried by the angels into Abraham’s bosom; the rich man also died, and was buried. And in hell he lift up his eyes, being in torments, and seeth Abraham afar off, and Lazarus in his bosom (Luk 16:23). He cried for Lazarus to cool his tongue, for he was tormented in this flame; but Abraham answered that between us and you there is a great gulf fixed, so that they which would pass from hence to you cannot (Luk 16:26). The rich man then begged that Lazarus warn his five brethren, but was told, They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them (Luk 16:29). The dictionary marks this account as our Lord’s own plain teaching upon the state of the dead. He sets before us conscious bliss for the believing poor and conscious torment for the unbelieving rich, a gulf fixed and impassable, and the sufficiency of the written Word. So the Scripture teaches that the soul lives on past death in joy or in woe, that there is no passing over from the one estate to the other, and that they who will not hear Moses and the prophets, neither will be persuaded though one rose from the dead.
webster_summary: Our Lord’s account of the rich man in torment and the beggar in Abraham’s bosom, with the great gulf fixed between.
webster_full: THE RICH MAN AND LAZARUS, our Lord’s account of two men in the state after death.
The rich man fared sumptuously, while Lazarus the beggar lay at his gate.
Lazarus was carried into Abraham’s bosom; the rich man lift up his eyes in torments.
A great gulf is fixed, so that none may pass from the one estate to the other.
Abraham bids the lost trust Moses and the prophets, the written Word.
scriptures: And it came to pass, that the beggar died, and was carried by the angels into Abraham’s bosom: the rich man also died, and was buried;
And in hell he lift up his eyes, being in torments, and seeth Abraham afar off, and Lazarus in his bosom.
And beside all this, between us and you there is a great gulf fixed: so that they which would pass from hence to you cannot; neither can they pass to us, that would come from thence.
And he said unto him, If they hear not Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded, though one rose from the dead.
corruption_summary: The denial of eternal conscious punishment, treating Christ’s account as “just a parable” to evade His plain teaching.
corruption_paragraphs: A real corruption of this passage is the denial of eternal conscious punishment, whether by the annihilationist who would have the lost extinguished, or by the universalist who teaches that God will eventually save all and empty hell at the last. To escape the plain force of our Lord’s words, the corruption styles this account “just a parable,” as though a parable might not teach truth, and so dismisses the torment, the flame, and the great gulf fixed as mere imagery carrying no doctrine of the world to come.

The dictionary rebuts this on the text and on the authority of Christ Himself. Whether this be a true history or a parable, it is the Lord’s own teaching, and He does not teach by falsehood; the conscious torment, the lifting up of the eyes, the cry for one drop of water, the memory and the longing, are set before us by Him who knoweth the state of the dead. He says plainly that the gulf is fixed, so that none may pass over; there is no second chance, no purgatorial cleansing, no final restoration. The plea that God’s love would not allow such a thing is not Scripture but sentiment set against Scripture; the same Christ who is the Saviour is the Judge, and His word here stands. The lost are warned, while the day of grace lasts, to hear Moses and the prophets, for after death the gulf cannot be crossed.
roots_summary: From the Greek account of Lazarus and the rich man, teaching conscious bliss and conscious torment after death.
roots_lines: The Rich Man and Lazarus — Lazarus, from Hebrew Eleazar, “God hath helped.”
Our Lord sets two men before us in the state after death.
Lazarus rests in Abraham’s bosom; the rich man is in torments.
A great gulf is fixed, impassable from either side.
They who hear not Moses and the prophets will not be persuaded though one rose.
usage: As in the account of the rich man and Lazarus, the soul lives on past death in joy or in woe.
Between us and you there is a great gulf fixed: so that they which would pass cannot.
If they hear not Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded though one rose from the dead.

etymology: From Greek oikonomos, “a manager of a household,” the parable of the steward accused of wasting his lord’s goods.
biblical_def: Our Lord spake of a certain rich man which had a steward; and the same was accused unto him that he had wasted his goods (Luk 16:1). Called to give account and put out of his stewardship, the man said within himself, I cannot dig; to beg I am ashamed (Luk 16:3); and so, while yet he held the office, he called his lord’s debtors and shrewdly lessened their bonds, that they might receive him into their houses when he was put out. And the lord commended the unjust steward, because he had done wisely: for the children of this world are in their generation wiser than the children of light (Luk 16:8). The dictionary marks this hard parable carefully. Our Lord praises not the steward’s dishonesty, but his foresight, that he used the goods passing through his hands to provide for the time to come; and He bids His own, Make to yourselves friends of the mammon of unrighteousness; that, when ye fail, they may receive you into everlasting habitations (Luk 16:9). The lesson is faithful stewardship of the wealth God lends, spent now with a view to eternity. So the Scripture teaches that earthly goods are a trust, to be used for the kingdom and for mercy; and our Lord seals all with the great word, ye cannot serve God and mammon (Luk 16:13). The heart must choose its lord, and the use of mammon shows which lord it has chosen.
webster_summary: The parable of the steward who used his lord’s goods with foresight, teaching prudent stewardship with a view to eternity.
webster_full: THE UNJUST STEWARD, the parable of a manager accused of wasting his lord’s goods.
Put out of his office, he provided for himself by lessening the debtors’ bonds.
His lord commended him, not for fraud, but for foresight.
Our Lord bids His own use mammon now with a view to eternity.
Ye cannot serve God and mammon: the heart must choose its lord.
scriptures: Luk 16:1
And he said also unto his disciples, There was a certain rich man, which had a steward; and the same was accused unto him that he had wasted his goods.
Luk 16:8

He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much: and he that is unjust in the least is unjust also in much.
No servant can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon.
corruption_summary: A parable little redefined by the present age; the principle to recover is faithful stewardship of mammon with a view to eternity.
corruption_paragraphs: The parable of the unjust steward has drawn little redefinition from the present age, being chiefly a difficulty to interpreters rather than a target of corruption. The dictionary records it that the reader may not stumble at our Lord’s commendation of a dishonest man, but mark that He praises the foresight, not the fraud, and draws from it a lesson in prudent stewardship.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the faithful stewardship of mammon with a view to eternity. The children of this world are wiser in their generation than the children of light, spending their goods shrewdly for the time to come; and our Lord would have His own use the wealth He lends with a like foresight, making friends by it for the everlasting habitations. Earthly goods are a trust, not a possession; and the use of them lays bare the heart, for ye cannot serve God and mammon. He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much; and the believer is taught to hold his mammon loosely, as a steward who must give account, spending it for mercy and for the kingdom of God.
roots_summary: From the Greek for “a household manager,” the parable teaches prudent stewardship and the impossibility of serving two masters.
roots_lines: The Unjust Steward — from Greek oikonomos, “a household manager.”
A steward accused of wasting goods provides for his coming need.
His lord commends his foresight, not his dishonesty.
Our Lord bids us use mammon now with a view to eternity.

usage: Like the steward, use the mammon God lends with a view to the everlasting habitations.
He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much.

etymology: From Greek aphron, “without reason, senseless,” the parable of the man whose soul was required of him in the night.
biblical_def: When one besought our Lord to bid his brother divide the inheritance, Christ warned, Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man’s life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth (Luk 12:15); and He told a parable. The ground of a certain rich man brought forth plentifully, and he thought within himself, saying, What shall I do, because I have no room where to bestow my fruits? (Luk 12:17). He resolved to pull down his barns and build greater, and to lay up all his goods, and said to his soul, Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years; take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry (Luk 12:19). But God said unto him, Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided? (Luk 12:20). The dictionary marks this parable as our Lord’s exposure of covetousness, that practical atheism which lays up treasure for self and is not rich toward God. The rich man’s folly was not in his harvest but in his heart: he reckoned without God, without death, and without his soul. So the Scripture teaches that the abundance of this life cannot secure it, and that a sudden summons may strip the covetous of all. So is he that layeth up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God (Luk 12:21).
webster_summary: The parable of the prosperous man whose soul was required the same night, exposing the folly of covetousness.
webster_full: THE RICH FOOL, the parable our Lord told to warn against covetousness.
His ground brought forth plentifully, and he planned greater barns.
He bade his soul take ease, eat, drink, and be merry for many years.
God said, Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee.
So is he that layeth up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God.
scriptures: And he said unto them, Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man’s life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth.
And I will say to my soul, Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years; take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry.
But God said unto him, Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided?
So is he that layeth up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God.
corruption_summary: A parable little redefined by the present age; the principle to recover is that covetousness is folly and a man must be rich toward God.
corruption_paragraphs: The parable of the rich fool has drawn little redefinition from the present age, though its warning is little heeded in an age that measures life by abundance. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark our Lord’s plain judgment upon the covetous heart, which lays up treasure for self and reckons without God.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that covetousness is folly in the sight of God, and a man’s life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth. The rich man’s sin was not his harvest but his heart: he counted his soul his own, his years secured, his goods enough, and God shut out of all his reckoning. But the summons came that night, Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee; and the heaped barns availed nothing. So the believer is taught to hold this world’s goods with a loose hand, to lay up treasure in heaven, and above all to be rich toward God; for he that trusteth in his riches shall fall, and a sudden death may strip the covetous of every thing he called his own.
roots_summary: From the Greek for “senseless,” the parable names the covetous man a fool whose soul is required of him.
roots_lines: The Rich Fool — from Greek aphron, “without reason, senseless.”
His ground brought forth plentifully, and he planned greater barns.
He bade his soul take ease for many years.
God required his soul that very night.
He laid up treasure for himself, and was not rich toward God.
usage: Like the rich fool, the covetous man reckons without God, his soul, and the world to come.
Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man’s life consisteth not in abundance.
Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee.

etymology: From Greek anaideia, “importunity, shamelessness,” the parable our Lord joined to His teaching on prayer.
biblical_def: Having taught His disciples to pray, our Lord set forth a parable to encourage them to persevere. Which of you shall have a friend, and shall go unto him at midnight, and say, Friend, lend me three loaves; for a friend of mine in his journey is come to me, and I have nothing to set before him? (Luk 11:5; Luk 11:6). And he within answers, Trouble me not: the door is now shut, and my children are with me in bed; I cannot rise and give thee (Luk 11:7). Yet our Lord declares, Though he will not rise and give him, because he is his friend, yet because of his importunity he will rise and give him as many as he needeth (Luk 11:8). The dictionary marks this parable as our Lord’s lesson in importunity, the persevering pressing of prayer that will not be put off. The argument is from the lesser to the greater: if a grudging neighbour, broken from his rest, will yield to a friend’s persistence, how much more shall the willing God answer His children who cry to Him. So our Lord adds, Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened (Luk 11:9). The Scripture teaches that God would have His people pray on, not because He must be wearied into answering, but because importunate prayer is the appointed means by which He gives, and the school in which faith is tried.
webster_summary: The parable of the man who gained bread at midnight by importunity, teaching perseverance in prayer.
webster_full: THE FRIEND AT MIDNIGHT, the parable our Lord joined to His teaching on prayer.
A man goes to his friend at midnight to borrow three loaves.
The friend within is unwilling, for the door is shut and his children abed.
Yet because of his importunity he rises and gives as many as he needeth.
So our Lord bids us ask, and seek, and knock, and persevere.

Luk 11:8

Luk 11:9

For every one that asketh receiveth; and he that seeketh findeth; and to him that knocketh it shall be opened.
corruption_summary: A parable little redefined by the present age; the principle to recover is importunity in prayer, the bold and persevering pressing upon God.
corruption_paragraphs: The parable of the friend at midnight has drawn little redefinition from the present age, being a homely lesson in perseverance rather than a battleground of doctrine. The dictionary records it that the reader may not mistake its argument, as though God were the grudging neighbour who must be wearied into giving, but mark the lesson from the lesser to the greater.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is importunity in prayer, the bold and persevering pressing upon God that will not be denied. If a friend broken from his sleep will yet rise for sheer persistence, how much more will the willing Father give good things to them that ask Him. The parable does not teach that God is reluctant, but that importunate prayer is the appointed means by which He bestows, and the school in which faith is exercised. So the believer is taught to ask, and seek, and knock, and not to faint; for every one that asketh receiveth, and the door is opened to him that perseveres in knocking.
roots_summary: From the Greek for “importunity,” the parable teaches the bold and persevering prayer that presses upon God.
roots_lines: The Friend at Midnight — from Greek anaideia, “importunity, shamelessness.”
A man borrows three loaves of his friend at midnight.
The friend within is unwilling, but yields to his persistence.
The argument runs from the grudging neighbour to the willing God.
Our Lord bids us ask, and seek, and knock, and persevere.
usage: Like the friend at midnight, the saint is taught to press his suit and not be put off.
Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened.

etymology: From Latin importunus, “unrelenting, pressing,” the parable rendering the widow who would not cease her plea before the unjust judge.
biblical_def: Our Lord spake a parable unto this end, that men ought always to pray, and not to faint (Luk 18:1). There was in a city a judge, which feared not God, neither regarded man; and a widow came unto him, saying, Avenge me of mine adversary (Luk 18:3). And he would not for a while; but afterward he said within himself, Though I fear not God, nor regard man, yet because this widow troubleth me, I will avenge her, lest by her continual coming she weary me (Luk 18:5). Then the Lord pressed it home: And shall not God avenge his own elect, which cry day and night unto him? (Luk 18:7). The dictionary marks this parable as our Lord’s great encouragement to persevering prayer, set against the temptation to faint in the long delay of answer. The argument runs from the lesser to the greater: if an unjust judge, moved by no fear of God, will yet right a widow for her ceaseless coming, how much more shall the righteous God avenge His own elect who cry to Him day and night. So the Scripture teaches that delay is not denial, that God bears long with His people for their good, and that He will avenge them speedily when His time is full. Yet our Lord closes with a searching word, Nevertheless when the Son of man cometh, shall he find faith on the earth? (Luk 18:8), warning that never-fainting prayer is the mark He seeks at His coming.
webster_summary: The parable of the widow whose ceaseless plea moved an unjust judge, teaching that men ought always to pray, and not to faint.
webster_full: THE IMPORTUNATE WIDOW, the parable that men ought always to pray, and not to faint.
A widow cried to an unjust judge, Avenge me of mine adversary.
He would not for a while, but yielded to her continual coming.
Shall not God avenge his own elect, which cry day and night unto him?
When the Son of man cometh, shall he find faith on the earth?

corruption_summary: A parable little redefined by the present age; the principle to recover is that men ought always to pray, and not to faint.
corruption_paragraphs: The parable of the importunate widow has drawn little redefinition from the present age, its plain end being stated by our Lord Himself. The dictionary records it that the reader may not mistake its argument, as though God were the unjust judge who must be wearied into doing right, but mark the lesson from the lesser to the greater.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that men ought always to pray, and not to faint. If an unjust judge, fearing neither God nor man, will yet avenge a widow for her ceaseless coming, how much more shall the righteous God avenge His own elect who cry day and night unto Him. The long delay is not denial, but the bearing-long of God with His people, that their faith may be tried and their crying continued; and He will avenge them speedily when His time is come. So the believer is armed against the temptation to grow weary, and warned by our Lord’s closing question, when the Son of man cometh, shall He find faith on the earth, that persevering, never-fainting prayer is the very mark of the faith He seeks.
roots_summary: From the Latin for “unrelenting,” the parable teaches the persevering prayer that cries day and night and faints not.
roots_lines: The Importunate Widow — from Latin importunus, “unrelenting, pressing.”
Our Lord told it that men ought always to pray, and not to faint.
A widow’s ceaseless plea moved an unjust judge.

usage: Like the importunate widow, the saint cries day and night and does not faint.
Men ought always to pray, and not to faint.

etymology: From Greek telones, “a tax-gatherer,” the parable our Lord spake to them which trusted in themselves that they were righteous.
biblical_def: Our Lord spake this parable unto certain which trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and despised others (Luk 18:9). Two men went up into the temple to pray; the one a Pharisee, and the other a publican. The Pharisee stood and prayed thus with himself, God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even as this publican (Luk 18:11); and he rehearsed his fastings and his tithes. But the publican, standing afar off, would not lift up so much as his eyes unto heaven, but smote upon his breast, saying, God be merciful to me a sinner (Luk 18:13). And our Lord pronounced the verdict: I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other (Luk 18:14). The dictionary marks this parable as our Lord’s plainest picture of justification, the great doctrine of how a sinner is accounted righteous before God. The Pharisee, trusting in his own works, went away unaccepted; the publican, despairing of himself and casting all upon mercy, went down justified. So the Scripture teaches that no man is justified by his own righteousness, by fasting or tithing or comparison with worse men, but the broken and contrite sinner who pleads only the mercy of God in Christ is freely accounted righteous. And our Lord seals it with the abiding rule of the kingdom: every one that exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted (Luk 18:14).
webster_summary: The parable of two men praying, in which the self-righteous Pharisee is rejected and the penitent publican goes down justified.
webster_full: THE PHARISEE AND THE PUBLICAN, the parable spoken to them that trusted in their own righteousness.

The Pharisee thanked God that he was not as other men.
The publican smote his breast, saying, God be merciful to me a sinner.
The publican went down to his house justified rather than the other.

corruption_summary: A parable little redefined by the present age; the principle to recover is justification by mercy alone, not by self-righteousness.
corruption_paragraphs: The parable of the Pharisee and the publican has drawn little redefinition from the present age, though its sharpest edge, the rejection of all self-righteousness, is forever unwelcome to the natural heart. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark our Lord’s own picture of justification, how a sinner is accounted righteous before God.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is justification by mercy alone, not by works or by self-righteousness. The Pharisee trusted in himself, his fasting, his tithing, his being better than other men, and went home unaccepted; the publican, despairing of his own worth and pleading only, God be merciful to me a sinner, went down justified. So the Scripture overthrows every confidence in the flesh and teaches that the broken and contrite sinner, casting himself wholly upon the mercy of God in Christ, is freely reckoned righteous. And the abiding rule of the kingdom stands over all: every one that exalteth himself shall be abased, and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted; for God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble.
roots_summary: From the Greek for “a tax-gatherer,” the parable teaches that the penitent sinner pleading mercy is justified, not the self-righteous.
roots_lines: The Pharisee and the Publican — from Greek telones, “a tax-gatherer.”

The Pharisee trusted in his own righteousness and was not accepted.
The publican pleaded, God be merciful to me a sinner.

etymology: From Greek chreopheiletes, “a debtor,” the parable our Lord spake in the house of Simon the Pharisee.
biblical_def: When a woman that was a sinner washed our Lord’s feet with her tears, and wiped them with the hairs of her head, and anointed them, Simon the Pharisee judged within himself that Christ could be no prophet to suffer it (Luk 7:38; Luk 7:39). In answer the Lord told him a parable. There was a certain creditor which had two debtors: the one owed five hundred pence, and the other fifty. And when they had nothing to pay, he frankly forgave them both. Tell me therefore, which of them will love him most? (Luk 7:41; Luk 7:42). Simon answered, I suppose that he, to whom he forgave most. And Christ said, Thou hast rightly judged (Luk 7:43); then turning to the woman He declared, Her sins, which are many, are forgiven; for she loved much: but to whom little is forgiven, the same loveth little (Luk 7:47). The dictionary marks this parable as our Lord’s lesson upon the love that springs from pardon. Both debtors owed what they could not pay, and were forgiven of free grace; and the greater the debt remitted, the greater the love that answered it. So the Scripture teaches that love to God is the fruit, not the price, of forgiveness; that the woman’s tears flowed because she was pardoned, not in order to be pardoned; and that the cold heart, like Simon’s, betrays a soul that has felt little of its own great debt. The sense of much forgiven kindles much love.
webster_summary: The parable of two debtors freely forgiven, teaching that to whom little is forgiven, the same loveth little.

corruption_paragraphs: The parable of the two debtors has drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as our Lord’s gentle and piercing word to a self-righteous host. The dictionary records it that the reader may not invert its order, as though the woman’s love purchased her pardon, but mark that her love flowed because she was forgiven.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that love to God is the fruit, and not the price, of forgiveness. Both debtors owed what they could not pay, and were freely forgiven of grace; and the greater the debt remitted, the greater the love that answered. The woman’s tears were the overflow of a pardoned heart, not the wage by which pardon was bought; for her sins, which were many, were forgiven, and therefore she loved much. Simon’s coldness betrayed a man who had felt little of his own great debt and little of the grace that cancels it. So the Scripture teaches that a deep sense of much forgiven kindles much love, and that the measure of our love to Christ is the measure of our wonder at His free and full forgiveness.

etymology: From Greek suke, “a fig tree,” the parable our Lord spake to warn of judgment upon fruitlessness.
biblical_def: Our Lord, having called the men of His day to repent or likewise perish, spake this parable. A certain man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard; and he came and sought fruit thereon, and found none (Luk 13:6). Then said he unto the dresser of his vineyard, Behold, these three years I come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and find none: cut it down; why cumbereth it the ground? (Luk 13:7). And the dresser answered, Lord, let it alone this year also, till I shall dig about it, and dung it: and if not, then after that thou shalt cut it down (Luk 13:9). The dictionary marks this parable as our Lord’s solemn word upon the patience of God and the peril of barrenness. The fig tree is the man planted in the place of privilege, owing fruit unto God; the lord of the vineyard is God, who justly seeks the fruit His planting has a right to expect; and the dresser’s plea is the long-suffering that grants a further season of grace. So the Scripture teaches that God bears long with the fruitless, adding means upon means to provoke them to fruit; but that His patience is not endless, and the tree that still cumbers the ground shall at the last be cut down. Privilege without fruit invites the axe; and the day of grace has its bound. The barren professor is warned to bring forth the fruit of repentance while the season of mercy lasts.
webster_summary: The parable of the fig tree spared one more year, teaching God’s patience and the threat of judgment on fruitlessness.

If it still bear no fruit, then it shall be cut down.

The dictionary records it that the reader may hold together both its lessons, the patience of God who spares, and the justice of God who at the last cuts down the fruitless.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God bears long with the fruitless, yet His patience is not endless. The fig tree is the man planted in the place of privilege, owing fruit unto God; and the Lord of the vineyard justly seeks what His planting has a right to expect. The dresser’s plea, let it alone this year also, is the long-suffering that grants a further season of grace, adding means upon means to provoke the tree to fruit. But privilege without fruit invites the axe, and the day of grace, however lengthened, has its bound. So the barren professor is warned, not soothed: bring forth fruit meet for repentance while the season of mercy lasts, lest, after all God’s digging and dunging, the word go forth at the last, cut it down; why cumbereth it the ground?

etymology: From Greek doulos, “a bondservant,” the parable our Lord spake to Peter touching the forgiveness of a brother.
biblical_def: When Peter asked how oft he should forgive his brother, our Lord answered, Until seventy times seven (Mat 18:22), and told a parable of the kingdom. A king would take account of his servants; and one was brought which owed him ten thousand talents, a debt past all paying. Having nothing to pay, the servant besought patience; and the lord of that servant was moved with compassion, and loosed him, and forgave him the debt (Mat 18:27). But the same servant went out, and found one of his fellowservants, which owed him an hundred pence, and he took him by the throat, saying, Pay me that thou owest (Mat 18:28); and he cast him into prison. When his lord heard of it, he said, O thou wicked servant, shouldest not thou also have had compassion on thy fellowservant, even as I had pity on thee? (Mat 18:33); and he delivered him to the tormentors. The dictionary marks this parable as our Lord’s teaching upon the forgiveness that flows from being forgiven. The ten thousand talents are the sinner’s vast debt to God, freely cancelled of mercy; the hundred pence are the small wrongs a brother does us. So the Scripture teaches that he who has been forgiven so great a debt must himself forgive, and that an unforgiving heart proves it has never known the grace it professes. So likewise shall my heavenly Father do, if ye from your hearts forgive not every one his brother their trespasses (Mat 18:35).
webster_summary: The parable of the servant forgiven ten thousand talents who would not forgive a hundred pence, teaching that the forgiven must forgive.
webster_full: THE UNMERCIFUL SERVANT, the parable our Lord spake to Peter on forgiving a brother.

His lord, moved with compassion, freely forgave him all the debt.
But he seized a fellowservant owing a hundred pence and cast him into prison.
His lord delivered the unmerciful servant to the tormentors.

corruption_paragraphs: The parable of the unmerciful servant has drawn little redefinition from the present age, its lesson lying plain upon the surface. The dictionary records it that the reader may not soften its close, the delivering of the servant to the tormentors, but mark the searching truth that an unforgiving heart betrays a soul that has never truly tasted the grace it professes.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that he who has been forgiven much must himself forgive. The ten thousand talents are the sinner’s vast and unpayable debt to God, freely cancelled of pure mercy; the hundred pence are the small wrongs a brother does us. To take a fellowservant by the throat over so little, after being loosed of so much, is a wickedness that lays bare a heart untouched by grace. So the Scripture teaches that forgiving flows from being forgiven, and that the freely-pardoned must freely pardon, or prove their own profession empty. The warning stands solemn over every man: so likewise shall the heavenly Father do, if ye from your hearts forgive not every one his brother their trespasses.
